news.headline: A Baseball-Sized Moon Rover Was Inspired by Toys
news.body: A tiny Japanese rover called SORA-Q starts out as a ball about the size of a baseball. After landing on the moon, the ball splits open and each half becomes a wheel, with cameras popping up in the middle. Its designers worked with a toy company and borrowed ideas from transforming toys like Transformers. The little robot crawled around on its own for more than 90 minutes, taking pictures.

news.headline: How Astronomers Found Rings Around Uranus
news.body: In 1977, Uranus passed in front of a faraway star. Before the planet blocked it, the starlight dimmed five times, and it flickered five times again afterward. Astronomers realized Uranus has rings, just like Saturn! The rings are dark and hard to see, so a star's blinking was the clue that revealed them. This kind of event, when one space object passes in front of another, is called an occultation.

fun_fact: Uranus spins tilted on its side, like a ball rolling around the sun instead of spinning like a top. 🪐

this_day_in_history: On November 15, 1971, Intel introduced the 4004, one of the first tiny computer chips of its kind. Chips like it help power the computers and tablets we use today! 💻
did_you_know: Moon dust is so sharp and sticky that it clings to everything, which is one reason wheels and gears on moon robots need careful designs. 🌙
